item.title: Artificial Turf Installation
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Artificial turf fails for the same reason a real lawn does — what is underneath it. We excavate, then lay and compact an open-graded aggregate base that genuinely drains, and seam and infill the turf over the top. Built that way it sheds water faster than the clay it replaced, and it does not lift when the ground freezes and thaws all winter.

On homes that means the shaded strip where grass has never taken, pet runs, poolside and small yards nobody wants to mow. On commercial sites it is playgrounds, putting greens, rooftop terraces, medians and HOA common ground — anywhere the maintenance budget is the problem rather than the planting.

item.title: Landscaping in Jackson Township
item.content:encoded:
Jackson Township wraps around the boroughs of Zelienople and Harmony, about fifteen minutes west of our yard in Cranberry. Lots here run larger than the Cranberry subdivisions and the housing stock is more mixed, which changes what a property needs.

Older homes sit on established ground with mature trees worth designing around, and drainage that was adequate for a smaller roof and a shorter driveway. Newer builds have the opposite problem: compacted subgrade and a thin skim of topsoil spread over it before the seed went down.

That split shows up in what we get called for. On the established side it is usually renovation — foundation beds planted too close to the house twenty years ago, a timber retaining wall that has finally given up, a wet corner that has been wet for as long as anyone remembers. On the newer side it is almost always the ground itself: decompaction, grading and a drainage fix before anything green is worth putting in.

Being fifteen minutes out matters more than it sounds. We can walk a property the same week you call, come back the next morning when a storm moves the schedule, and keep one crew on one job until it is finished rather than splitting them across the county. Jackson Township sits inside our normal working radius, so there is no travel premium on anything quoted here.

Timing matters more here than it does on a small lot. Spring and early autumn book out first, because that is when sod, seed and planting take best and a larger property takes longer to turn around than a courtyard. Drainage and hardscape work we can usually start sooner — wet ground is the problem we are there to solve, not a reason to wait for it to dry out.

That split decides the work. In the south we are usually correcting what was left behind: decompaction, grading, a drainage fix, then a patio or a lawn worth having. Further north it is hydroseeding across open ground, stone work on driveways and access, and structures built far enough from the house that lighting stops being decorative and starts being how people find the door.

item.title: Landscaping in Allegheny County
item.content:encoded:
Allegheny County is our southern market, and the terrain changes character as soon as you cross the line. The North Hills is genuinely hilly, and slope drives almost every decision on a property — where a patio can physically sit, how many tiers a wall needs, and where the water coming off the ground above you is going to end up.

The housing stock is mature. A lot of what we do here is renovation rather than installation: taking out foundation shrubs planted too close to the house when it was built, rebuilding timber retaining walls that have finally rotted through, and re-cutting bed lines that have crept outward for twenty years.

Tree cover is the other constant. Pine, Marshall, McCandless and Hampton carry serious canopy, which means shade where turf will not establish, root competition in every bed, and enough leaf load to kill a lawn over winter if it sits. Shade-tolerant seed blends, selective canopy work and, where grass genuinely will not grow, artificial turf all get used here.

In Sewickley, Fox Chapel and Franklin Park the finish standard is higher and the deer pressure is heavier. A beautifully planned bed of hostas and arborvitae is a feeding station in those neighbourhoods, so plant selection is deliberate and anything the deer will take gets protected through its establishment years.

We work the City of Pittsburgh itself too, mostly the northern neighbourhoods and mostly on larger projects where the travel is justified — city lots bring access limits, permits, and neighbours close enough that cleaning the site every evening is not optional.

Lots here are not large, which changes the brief rather than shrinking it. Every square foot has to earn its place, and the difference between a good Cranberry garden and a poor one is usually how carefully the hard and soft areas were divided up.

Houses here are newer and substantial, and they were typically handed over with a rear yard that is flat, seeded and completely empty. The land was graded to move water off it, which is not the same as grading it to be used.

Planting plans here have to account for time. The trees are young, so a bed designed for the shade that exists today will be wrong in eight years. We plant for what the canopy becomes rather than what it is.

New Brighton sits on the Beaver River with Daugherty Township around it, and the combination of older housing and valley gradient produces a consistent set of problems.

Drainage is the most common first job. Systems here were sized for smaller roofs and shorter driveways than are now feeding into them, and on sloping ground that shortfall shows up quickly after heavy rain.

Gradient means level outdoor space is built. Retaining work appears in most projects, and terracing usually beats a single tall wall both structurally and in how much usable ground it leaves.

Period frontages suit natural stone and planting scaled to the building rather than contemporary schemes designed for new builds. On compact lots everything is visible at once, which makes restraint more valuable than variety.
